sources.title: NGSS 4-LS1-2: Use a model to describe that animals receive different types of information through their senses, process the information in their brain, and respond to the information in different ways

note.text: Your eyes take in information about the world as light, so you can see what's around you.

steps.title: Cornea
steps.instruction: Trace the clear bulge at the front.

note.text: The cornea is the clear front of the eye. It protects the eye and starts bending light so you can see clearly.

steps.title: Iris
steps.instruction: Draw the iris, leaving the gap of the pupil between.

note.text: The iris is the colored ring of your eye. It makes the pupil, the hole in the middle, smaller in bright light and bigger in dim light.
note.remember: Iris controls how much light enters.

steps.title: Lens
steps.instruction: Trace the lens behind the iris.

note.text: The lens focuses light onto the back of the eye. It changes shape to focus on things near and far.

steps.title: Retina
steps.instruction: Trace the retina lining the back of the eye.

note.text: The retina turns light into signals, a bit like a camera's sensor.

steps.title: Optic nerve
steps.instruction: Draw the optic nerve running to the brain.

note.text: The optic nerve carries the signals from the retina to your brain.
Your brain makes sense of the signals: it works out what you're seeing, then decides how you respond.

steps.title: Light
steps.instruction: Draw the arrow of light coming into the eye.

note.text: You see an object when light from it enters your eye.

steps.title: From light to brain
steps.instruction: Tap the parts in the order light and its signals reach them.
steps.why: Light passes the cornea, goes through the pupil, is focused by the lens onto the retina, and the optic nerve carries the signals to the brain.
steps.hint: What's at the very front of the eye?

steps.title: Respond
steps.question: You walk from a dark room into bright sunshine. What does your eye do?

options.text: The iris makes the pupil smaller to let in less light
options.feedback: Yes. In bright light the iris shrinks the pupil, letting less light in. It happens without you even thinking about it.
Pupils get bigger in dim light, to let more light in. In bright light they shrink.
The lens stays put. The iris changes the size of the pupil.
Your eye responds: the iris makes the pupil smaller in bright light.
